newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH PM NOT TO AVOID TOUGH ISSUES IN RUSSIA.
newsitem.headline: POLISH PM NOT TO AVOID TOUGH ISSUES IN RUSSIA.

text.p: Poland's Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, leaving for Moscow on Tuesday, said he would not avoid tough issues of European security during talks with Russian leaders.
He told reporters he would sign agreements, including one settling mutual trade debts left from the communist era, and would discuss plans to prepare an easing of bilateral trade.
"I also think this will be a good chance to talk about difficult issues, among others security matters," he said.
Cimoszewicz said he expected the Russians to stress external, European security while he was most concerned with the problem of spreading international crime.
The main irritant in bilateral ties is Russia's opposition to neighbouring Poland's plans to fully join NATO fast.
Moscow denounces the pact's enlargement as a potential threat, while some Polish officials suspect Russia's concern is to retain a traditional sphere of influence embracing Poland.
Cimoszewicz said NATO enlargement was not up to Poland and Russia to decide, but he wanted to hear Russia's objections.
"In my view there are no serious substantial counter arguments," Cimoszewicz added.
He said an enlarged NATO, its ties with Russia regulated by special agreements, had to play a key role in Europe.

Poland, which was occupied by Russia throughout the 19th century and escaped Soviet domination in 1989, is anxious that Russia pressure should not persuade NATO states to dilute the full guarantees which Warsaw seeks from pact membership.

"I would like the main message of this visit reaching the ordinary Russian to be that Poland wants good relations with Russia, we want to cooperate, but that we don't forget we also have rights," he said.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Davydov has suggested a free-trade zone between the two countries, which Poland has said it cannot now agree to because of effects on its other partners, especially the European Union it wants to join.

Poland is, however, interested in easing barriers to trade with Russia where possible. Cimoszewicz said a memorandum had been prepared, suggesting studies by a joint team of experts. but final details of its form had not been decided yet.

He said negotiating a deal freeing trade would be highly complex and would have to take account of concerns by members of the EU, Poland's chief trading partner, whose Warsaw ambassadors last week said they expected to be fully consulted.

Cimoszewicz, following up a Moscow visit by President Aleksander Kwasniewski in April, will meet Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and other top officials on Wednesday, visit St Petersburg for business-related talks and go on to Tatarstan to discuss trade and oil imports from the autonomous republic.
He is not scheduled to meet President Boris Yeltsin, recovering from heart surgery, but will see Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais during the trip ending on Friday.
